short: Mei says the kettle had barely gone cold when you came back.
Mei says she kept the stall open and no one waited in the dark.
Mei says a few regulars stopped by and left with warm hands.
Mei says she opened early out of habit, though you were only gone a moment.
evening: Mei says she opened before the lanterns were lit, and a line was already waiting.
Mei says the regulars came in out of the cold and stayed for a second cup.
Mei says the kettle sang all evening and she never let it run dry.

long: Mei says the lanterns were lit, burned low, and the kettle was still warm.
Mei says the whole night passed and she was first to open again before dawn.
Mei says she poured until the lane went quiet, then put the kettle on once more.

short: Bo says he started a story, and a few regulars were already listening.
Bo says the steamer was still warm when you came back.
Bo says he folded a few dumplings and talked through every one.
Bo says he did not lose a single fold, though he never stopped talking.
evening: Bo says the regulars stayed to hear the end of his story, and the dumplings kept coming.
Bo says he talked while he folded and never lost track of a pleat.
Bo says the steamer was filled and emptied while he told the whole story again.

long: Bo says he talked until the lane went quiet, and his hands kept folding all the while.
Bo says the regulars stayed to listen long after the last dumpling was gone.
Bo says he told a story, then another, and folded through both.
Bo says the steam rose all night while he talked.

short: An says the flames sat still the whole time you were gone.
An says she trimmed one more wick, and the flame did not so much as flicker.
An says nothing needed her but one patient wick.
An says the lantern light stayed steady.
evening: An says she trimmed each wick until its flame stood still.
An says the lamps burned clean while the lane filled up.
An says a few moths came to look and found only a calm flame.
An says she walked the poles at dusk, trimming each wick in turn.
long: An says the wicks burned clean all night, and she trimmed them again at dawn.
An says the flames never wavered, though the night was long.
An says the whole alley stayed lit and not one flame needed hurrying.
An says she trimmed wick after wick until the alley glowed softly.

short: Qiao says she counted the tins, then counted them again, just to be sure.
Qiao says only one tin left the table, and it was the one she liked least.
Qiao says every tin was still in its row when you came back.
Qiao says she kept counting and nobody rushed her.
evening: Qiao says she counted the tins at dusk and again at dark, and they matched.
Qiao says the tin she liked least was the first one asked for.
Qiao says she wrapped each mooncake slowly while the lane filled.
Qiao says she lined up the tins again and kept the best one for later.
long: Qiao says she counted the tins so many times that the lane began to tease her.
Qiao says every tin the lane asked for was the one she liked least.
Qiao says she wrapped, counted and wrapped again until the night grew late.
Qiao says the table was never empty, and the best tin stayed hers.

short: Ren says he lit one stick for the stall and one for the alley.
Ren says the smoke was still curling when you came back.
Ren says the alley smelled welcome before anyone arrived.
Ren says he had only just set the second stick at the mouth of the alley.
evening: Ren says the alley stick burned down while the stall stick kept the tray warm.
Ren says visitors followed the smoke down the alley and found the tray.
Ren says he lit a fresh stick each time the old one went out.

long: Ren says he lit stick after stick through the night, one for the stall and one for the alley.
Ren says the alley smelled of cedar from dusk until the lamps burned low.
Ren says the smoke could be seen from the gate long after dark.
Ren says the ribbons of smoke never thinned, because he never let a stick burn out.

short: Old Wen says he began a story and stopped just before the ending.
Old Wen says the crowd leaned in and waited, and he let them.
Old Wen says the mat was still warm and the tale was still unfinished.
Old Wen says he told only the start, since you would want to hear the rest.
evening: Old Wen says the crowd begged for the rest, and he stopped just before the ending again.
Old Wen says the listeners brought tea and sat close for the middle of the tale.
Old Wen says he reached the edge of the ending, then paused to let the crowd wonder.
Old Wen says he told the story slowly, one breath at a time, and the crowd stayed.
long: Old Wen says the crowd stayed until the lanterns burned low, waiting for the ending.
Old Wen says he told the whole night's story and stopped, once more, just before the ending.
Old Wen says the crowd changed and changed again, and the tale was still not finished.
Old Wen says he saved the ending for you, and the crowd agreed to wait.
